summary: Solicits white papers on topics related to the requirements and selection criteria for IPng, the next generation of IP. It is a call for input, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet was getting crowded, and people asked for essays on what the next version should be like.

subtitle: A 1993 call for white papers on what the next version of IP should have to do.

tldr.problem: The IETF's IP: next generation (IPng) area needed outside input on the requirements for a new IP and on the factors that should influence which proposal was chosen.
tldr.mechanism: It invites anyone to submit white papers of up to 10 pages, sets a review process and format rules, and lists sixteen engineering topics as prompts.
tldr.outcome: It is a call for input, not a protocol. The deadline it gives was February 1, 1994, and submitted papers were to be published as informational RFCs.

today: RFC 1550 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a historical call for input whose deadline of February 1, 1994 has long passed.

sections.title: The Call for White Papers
sections.content:
The IPng area in the IETF asks all interested parties for white papers on IPng requirements and selection criteria. One example is a utility company describing the scaling and addressing it would need for utility meters. Another is a paper on the effect of wireless networks on IPng.

Papers that evaluate specific IPng proposals are not accepted yet. They would be accepted once the proposals were clear and complete. The deadline is February 1, 1994, and papers go to ipng-wp@harvard.edu.
sections.plainLanguage: The people picking the next Internet design said: tell us what you need from it, before we choose.

sections.title: Review and Publication
sections.content:
Each paper gets a clarity review by members of the IPng directorate and the external review board, then a separate technical review that assesses feasibility without making value judgments. Either may produce suggestions for the author.

Afterwards the paper is submitted as an Internet-Draft, and after a suitable period as an informational RFC unless the author withdraws it. These papers become part of the historical record of the IPng process.
sections.plainLanguage: Papers are checked to be clear and possible, then shared with everyone, like essays pinned on a board.

sections.title: Format Rules and Outline
sections.content:
Papers follow RFC 1543 format and must not exceed 10 pages. The reference version must be ASCII, with an optional PostScript copy. Each begins with an executive summary of no more than half a page, then covers the issues the author thinks matter. An author may submit more than one paper.

Appendix A copies the ASCII rules: 58 lines per page and 72 characters per line.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep it short, begin with a quick summary, and use plain text so every computer can read it.

sections.title: Suggested Engineering Topics
sections.content:
The RFC lists sixteen issues raised in earlier discussions, in no particular order: scaling, timescale, transition and deployment, security, configuration and operation, mobile hosts, flows and resource reservation, policy based routing, topological flexibility, applicability, datagram service, accounting, support of communication media, robustness and fault tolerance, technology pull, and action items.

On scaling, the current common wisdom is that IPng should deal with 10 to the 12th nodes. Timescale papers are forwarded to the ALE working group, and transition papers to the TACIT working group. The security section says the RFC raises no security issues but invites comment on security requirements of IPng.
sections.plainLanguage: It gives a checklist of things to think about, like how many computers there will be and how to move from the old design to the new one.
